title: Start a hotfix branch from the release, not from main
summary: Production runs v1.0. main has moved on by six commits of unreleased work. Branch from the right point so the hotfix ships without dragging unfinished features with it.
mental_model: A new branch starts wherever you point it, not where you happen to be standing. `git switch -c fix v1.0` means 'give me the world as it was at v1.0'. Getting this wrong is how unreleased features reach production inside a one-line fix.
danger: Branching a hotfix from main includes every unreleased commit on main. The pull request looks like one line; the deployment is not.

commit.message: More scheduling rewrite, not working yet

steps.title: See what main is carrying
steps.why: Three commits since the release, two of them explicitly unfinished. Anything branched from here inherits all of it.

steps.title: Branch from the tag, not from HEAD
steps.why: `switch -c <name> <start-point>` creates the branch at the start point and moves there. The working tree becomes exactly the released code — the experimental file is not even on disk.
steps.expect: No experimental.py, VERSION back to 1.0, one commit of history.

verify.label: the hotfix branch does not contain unreleased work

steps.title: Make the fix
steps.why: One commit, on top of the released code. Its parent is the release, so the diff against v1.0 is exactly the fix and nothing else.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Use constant-time comparison in auth check"

steps.expect: One file changed. That is the entire shipping surface.

verify.label: the branch changes exactly one file relative to the release

steps.title: Tag and ship the patch release
steps.why: A tag on the hotfix commit gives operations something to deploy by name. v1.0.1 contains v1.0 plus one fix, and nothing else — provable with a diff.

verify.label: the patch release differs from 1.0 by one file

steps.title: Merge the fix back into main
steps.why: The hotfix must also reach the development line, or the next release regresses it. Merging is right here — the fix's commit becomes reachable from main without main's work coming along to production.
commands: git merge --no-ff -m "Merge hotfix 1.0.1 into main" hotfix/auth-length

verify.label: main has the fix too
verify.hint: merge the hotfix branch back into main

steps.title: Compare with what would have happened
steps.why: Branching from main would have made the shipping diff include both experimental commits. Look at the difference in surface area — one file versus three.
steps.expect: main differs from the release by three files; the patch release by one.

steps.title: Other start points worth knowing
steps.why: Any revision works as a start point: a sha, a tag, `origin/main`, or `main~5`. Branching from `origin/main` rather than your possibly-stale local main is a habit worth building.

verify.label: the patch release contains exactly one changed file
verify.hint: branch the hotfix from v1.0, not from main

verify.label: the fix was merged back into main
the patch release is one commit ahead of the release it patches

pitfalls: `git switch -c fix` with no start point branches from wherever you are, which is usually main. Naming the start point is the whole discipline.
Cherry-picking the fix onto main instead of merging leaves two commits with the same content and different shas — harmless but confusing during audits.
Branching from a stale local main gives you yesterday's world. Use `origin/main` after a fetch when you mean 'what the server has'.
Tags do not move. If you re-cut a release, make a new tag rather than force-updating the old one.
cheatsheet: branch at a tag, sha or branch
